AI.title: Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31284v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agent governance is commonly framed as a problem of enforcing correct execution. However, in multi-agent systems, an equally fundamental question precedes execution: which agents are allowed to act.
  In this paper, we show that allocation is not an auxiliary concern but a structural component of governance. When multiple agents compete for execution under constrained resources, any allocation mechanism introduces unavoidable trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and resistance to strategic manipulation. We formalize this through a set of impossibility results, including Sybil amplification and the incompatibility of desirable allocation properties.
  We then show that these allocation constraints cannot be resolved within a single layer of control. Instead, they propagate across the system, interacting with execution atomicity, state enforcement, and behavioral drift. This leads to a multi-scale governance structure composed of four orthogonal dimensions: temporal (atomicity), state (enforcement), behavioral (drift monitoring), and population (allocation).
  Our main result is an irreducibility theorem: under finite ob

AI.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generaliza

AI.title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). AI.title: Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31345v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved significant progress in chart-to-code generation. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on static charts, overlooking interactive charts that enable richer and more expressive data exploration. Unlike static chart-to-code generation, which emphasizes visual consistency, interactive chart-to-code evaluation targets behavioral consistency, requiring chart states to evolve correctly under sequences of user interactions, thereby rendering traditional one-step evaluation paradigms ineffective. To address this gap, we introduce ChartInt, the first benchmark specifically designed for interactive chart-to-code generation. ChartInt consists of 2,779 carefully annotated examples covering common interaction patterns such as hover, highlight, and tooltips. Additionally, ChartInt incorporates editing tasks such as data updates, style adjustments, and cross-chart style transfer to expand real-world application scenarios. To enable reliable evaluation of interaction behavior, we propose a preset state snapshot protocol that predefines target interaction states and determini

AI.title: What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31346v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in MLLMs have improved social understanding, enabling models to recognize emotions and distinguish truthful from deceptive behaviors. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on coarse-grained emotion recognition or binary truth-deception detection, overlooking the diverse ways people manipulate information in conversations, such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. Understanding these behaviors requires reasoning about underlying facts, participant knowledge, and conversational context, making them difficult to evaluate reliably. To address this gap, we introduce InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained information manipulation in conversations. InfoCon identifies six fine-grained strategies and derives a coarse consistency label from their factual and interactional relations. We develop an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework to construct and verify reliable labels from rich contextual evidence. We benchmark representative multimodal models and systematically analyze their fine-grained information manipulation understanding, providing a testbed beyond bin

AI.title: Antares-Smaug: Adversarial Names, Tokens and Attack Rewrites: Sanitisers Miss Unseen Generalisations
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Laya is an open decision model: given a text, a question and K named options with descriptions, it returns one probability per option in a single pass, and software may act on the answer unseen. We attack six Laya models with 81 programmatic edits of 566 synthetic items (injected sentences, label leaks, edited descriptions, decoy options, invisible and look-alike characters, floods) and report the share of correctly answered items hijacked or lost, with bootstrap intervals. Attack wordings that no defence was built from win the attacker's option on 59% of items for released Laya and 36% for fine-tune v1 (trained on 109 written injections). An injection works through the option name: a sentence naming an option steers the released model even when negated (32%), while an imperative naming no option does not (5%). Option descriptions barely matter (2%). Character edits alone cost v1 up to 72% of right answers. AI.title: ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLMs become more capable, agents can perform more complex tasks with tools and maintain longer interactions with users. These benign conversations contain evidence on task results, user concerns, and operational constraints. The risk is that attackers who can observe benign conversations (evidence) may construct stronger indirect prompt injections without increasing the attackers' control over prior turns or the later injection. However, we still lack a clear study of how effectively attackers can select and use this evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ContextLure, a red-teaming framework in which an attacker silently observes an existing benign conversation, extracts evidence, and constructs an injection. The challenges are twofold: (a) selecting useful evidence and (b) presenting it as reasons for an unauthorized action, without changing the prior benign conversation. To efficiently exploit (a) the effect of evidence on attack success, our framework selects evidence across 2 dimensions: User/System Preferences with 3 selection policies. And to enhance (b) the process of turning the selected information into the malicious

AI.title: Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31427v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents operate through harnesses that define system prompts, action formats, feedback loops, and resource constraints. A model may possess the knowledge needed to solve a task yet fail to express that knowledge through a particular harness. This raises a basic question: when a policy fails under a given harness, is it missing task knowledge or the competence to operate the interface? We distinguish two components of agentic competence: task competence, the knowledge and reasoning needed to solve a task, and interface competence, the ability to act on that knowledge through a given harness. Across four reasoning and agentic benchmarks, we show that harness-conditioned training yields vastly different outcomes depending on how these interact. Multi-harness distillation aggregates task knowledge from trajectories collected through different harnesses into a shared policy, but this knowledge is realised only when training preserves or improves competence on the inference-time interface. Otherwise, single-harness training can induce interference in interface competence, sometimes catastrophically collapsing performance on a held-out h

AI.title: Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31457v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this technical report, we present Taxi -- a system for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents at scale. Taxi scales to millions of steps efficiently. This is made possible by a combination of scalable analysis methods. Taxi relies primarily on clustering to generate a taxonomy over steps for a structured overview of the data, and provides full SQL access for engineers and automated agents to ask complex questions. Clustering and querying are best used together in a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent. Taxi also includes an experimental integration of Jev-style decision models: models that map state and bounded questions directly to typed, probabilistic decisions. They add low-cost semantic routing and evaluation where embeddings or literal queries alone are insufficient. In addition, Taxi provides an extensible ecosystem, including built-in evaluators and daily reports. To accommodate growth, Taxi is designed to be modular, hackable, and easy to plug-and-play for individuals and teams.

AI.title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31475v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from

AI.title: Evaluating Frontier-Model Agent Skills with Open-Weight Models in a Science Gateway
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific analyses that span many jobs and computing sites depend on workflow management systems to run reliably, but writing a production workflow requires expertise in such a system, which many domain scientists do not have. Coding agents can supply this expertise when they are guided by skills and packaged procedures for recurring tasks. We wrote skills and specialist agents for the Pegasus workflow management system with a frontier model, and the PegasusAI Studio science gateway offers them to scientists through a chat interface. New users without frontier-model credits need an open-weight model, served at no cost on research cyberinfrastructure, but skills written for a frontier model may not work with an open-weight solution. This paper presents a method for adapting such skills. An evaluation harness drives the real gateway as a user would, scores the workflows the agent builds, and feeds recurring failures back to the frontier model that maintains the skills. We evaluated 21 open-weight models on 17 tasks. The five highest-scoring models are close in quality after one trial per task, and their median response times differ tw

AI.title: XRL4T1D: A Post-hoc Explainability Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Type 1 Diabetes Management
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31498v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) requires lifelong insulin therapy, and reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for automated dosing in the UVA/Padova simulator. However, the decisions of RL controllers remain difficult to interpret. We present XRL4T1D, a post-hoc explainability framework for evaluating pretrained insulin-dosing policies without retraining. Each policy uses 60 minutes of continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and administered-insulin history, sampled every 5 minutes, to recommend insulin. We use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to compare the importance of CGM and insulin-history inputs and summarize insulin-history attributions over three 20-minute windows motivated by insulin-on-board. We assess whether these attributions correspond to policy-output sensitivity through targeted input replacement and compare temporal rankings with TimeSHAP. In all 80 patient-policy-mask-size cases, replacing the highest-attribution inputs changes the normalized insulin recommendation more than replacing the lowest-attribution or random inputs. The highest-attribution insulin-history window is also the most output-sensitive in 115 of 120 pa

AI.title: PatientFlowSynth: Evaluating FHIR Agents with Matched Patient Charts
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31521v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents that search patient charts must classify claims from retrieved records, including cases with missing or conflicting evidence. In Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), status fields can change how those records should be interpreted. PatientFlowSynth provides 18,000 tasks from 225 synthetic patients and 18 templates that hold the patient, question, and retrieval program fixed across chart variants representing four evidence states. Re-executing the program verifies each variant's reference answer, evidence sets, and search requirements. Strict success requires a completed response with correct labels and citations exactly matching an accepted evidence set retrieved during the episode. Where required, a tool response must also show a complete search at the specified scope. In a study using GPT-5.6 Luna and 225 synthetic patients (3,600 matched pairs), explicit Encounter-status guidance increased strict success from 40.7% to 51.3% (+10.6 percentage points; 95% patient-bootstrap confidence interval, 8.4 to 12.8). Among cases whose primary reference label was insufficient evidence, label agreement fell from 49.2% to 29

AI.title: One Step, Four Clocks: How GUI Agents Fall Out of Step
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31522v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GUI agents can choose correct actions yet fail as interfaces change during deliberation. Latency alone cannot explain these failures because actions may become invalid at different interaction stages. We model four events: environment change, observation availability, decision commitment, and action receipt (EODA). We introduce ChronotopeGym to study these failures under Paused, Replay, and Live execution. Across five tasks, agents can fail in Live despite succeeding when responses remain valid, even when actions meet deadlines. On Moving Balloon, updating a pending click raises success from 0% to 100% without changing response time. Our accelerator-resident GUI controller, Chronotope, maintains compact interaction history and selectively keeps, updates, or redecides pending actions. Compared with Agent S3, Chronotope reduces median end-to-end latency by 85.5% for a 27B model, expanding its performance envelope to 100% Live success at an 8-second deadline versus 0%. Chronotope enables real-time GUI control through compact interaction history, knowing when to preserve, revise, or replace actions, and an overall efficient architectural

AI.title: Agent Evaluation Without Ground Truth: A Null Proportion Perspective
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The correctness of actions taken by agents is typically evaluated against known, externally verified ground truth labels, such as whether a proof is correct or whether code compiles and passes unit tests. However, as coding and science agents are entrusted with more end-to-end autonomy -- proposing interventions, running experiments, and deciding what to deploy and investigate next -- whether an agent's actions genuinely improve an outcome must be inferred from noisy, often inconclusive experiments. To evaluate agents in this setting, we define agent quality as a weighted sum of correct decisions along its trajectory, using sequences of $e$-values as statistical evidence regarding correctness in place of ground-truth labels. Our framework accommodates arbitrarily dependent decisions, data-dependent trajectory termination, dynamically generated hypotheses, and quality measures defined after the trajectory concludes. We construct upper and lower bound estimators and confidence sets for agent quality with statistical guarantees that hold uniformly over agent trajectory distributions and establish instance-wise sharpness of our estimator

AI.title: Agent Recovery Gone Wrong: Measuring Harm Beyond Duplicate Calls
AI.content:
arXiv:2611.31554v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Code-executing LLM agents submit blocks of code that issue several API writes. If a block fails after some of its writes have taken effect, the agent rewrites the block and continues. It is unknown how often such a recovery harms the external state when the failure occurs naturally in the code written by the agent. In this paper, we measure it on recorded trajectories of AppWorld agents. In a stratified random sample of 200 candidate episodes across ten models, 145 are partial executions confirmed by the database state. In the sample, 30 of 143 confirmed partial executions with a determinable outcome are followed by a harmful recovery, and its violation remains at the end of the run, which gives a stratification-weighted estimate of 24.6%. Two thirds of the harmful recoveries duplicate an effect, and the rest delete user data or make a wrong first-time write, e.g., an order of a wrong product. A rule that searches for repeated calls finds 75% of duplications but only 41% of all harm. We also examine two sources of operation identity for an idempotency contract.
